triage.name: Retinopathy of prematurity
triage.reason: Premature infant found on screening fundoscopic exam; diagnosis is made by eye exam rather than interview, so it is a weaker but still usable case.

demographics: Occurs almost exclusively in infants born prematurely; risk rises as gestational age and birth weight fall
More common in infants of lower gestational age and lower birth weight, and in those who received supplemental oxygen
Slightly more common in male infants in some series

risk_factors.text: Prematurity, especially birth before 30–32 weeks gestation
Low birth weight, especially under 1500 g
Supplemental oxygen therapy or prolonged mechanical ventilation
Very low gestational age at birth
Neonatal sepsis, intraventricular hemorrhage, or necrotizing enterocolitis

exposures: Supplemental oxygen in the neonatal period

chief_complaints.text: The NICU team said my baby needs an eye exam because she was born early
My baby doesn't seem to follow my face or the light the way I expected

hpi.onset: Detected on routine screening eye examination in the neonatal period, typically 4–6 weeks after birth or around 31–33 weeks postmenstrual age
hpi.duration: Present since the neonatal period; may progress over weeks to months if untreated
hpi.progression: Often asymptomatic and found only on screening; if it progresses, retinal changes advance through stages and can lead to retinal detachment and vision loss
hpi.quality: Painless; no symptoms noticed by the infant
hpi.severity: Variable; most cases are mild and regress, but severe cases can cause blindness
hpi.timing: Screening occurs at fixed postnatal/postmenstrual ages; progression is monitored over weeks

associated_symptoms.text: No visual response to faces or objects

atypical.how_it_differs: Most infants are completely asymptomatic; the condition is found only on screening examinations. Even advanced disease may cause no obvious signs until vision loss is severe.
Older children with a history of prematurity may present with strabismus, nystagmus, poor vision, or leukocoria if the disease was not detected or treated in infancy.

general.mild: Premature infant, alert and feeding, no external eye abnormality; ROP found only on screening examination
general.moderate: Premature infant, otherwise stable; abnormal retinal vascular findings on dilated fundoscopy
general.severe: Premature infant with plus disease or stage 3 ROP; may have poor visual tracking or nystagmus
general.critical: Infant with retinal detachment or leukocoria; may be lethargic or feeding poorly if systemically unwell

findings.maneuver: Perform dilated indirect ophthalmoscopy and examine the peripheral retina
findings.finding: A thin, flat, white line separating vascularized from avascular retina (stage 1 ROP)

findings.maneuver: Perform dilated indirect ophthalmoscopy and examine the peripheral retina
findings.finding: An elevated ridge of tissue at the junction of vascularized and avascular retina (stage 2 ROP)

findings.maneuver: Perform dilated indirect ophthalmoscopy and examine the peripheral retina
findings.finding: Fibrovascular proliferation extending from the ridge into the vitreous (stage 3 ROP)

findings.maneuver: Perform dilated indirect ophthalmoscopy and assess the posterior retinal vessels
findings.finding: Marked dilation and tortuosity of the posterior retinal vessels (plus disease)

findings.maneuver: Perform dilated indirect ophthalmoscopy and examine the peripheral retina
findings.finding: Partial or total retinal detachment (stage 4 or 5 ROP)

findings.maneuver: Inspect the red reflex with a direct ophthalmoscope or observe the pupillary light reflex
Assess ocular alignment with the corneal light reflex or cover test
Observe the eyes for involuntary rhythmic movements
Present a face or bright object and observe whether the infant fixes and follows
findings.finding: Failure to fix and follow (poor visual tracking)

findings.maneuver: Inspect the cornea, iris, lens, and conjunctiva with a penlight and direct ophthalmoscope
findings.finding: Clear cornea, normal iris, clear lens, no conjunctival injection or discharge

findings.maneuver: Check the red reflex in both eyes with a direct ophthalmoscope
Perform dilated fundoscopy to examine the posterior segment

imaging.preferred_when: All infants meeting ROP screening criteria, and every follow-up until retinal vascularization is complete

findings.text: Thin flat white line separating vascularized from avascular retina (stage 1)
Elevated ridge of tissue at the junction of vascularized and avascular retina (stage 2)
Fibrovascular proliferation extending from the ridge into the vitreous (stage 3)
Marked dilation and tortuosity of posterior retinal vessels (plus disease)
Partial or total retinal detachment (stage 4 or 5)
Immature, incompletely vascularized peripheral retina without demarcation line or ridge

imaging.preferred_when: When the retina cannot be visualized directly because of media opacity or poor pupillary dilation

findings.text: Retinal detachment not visible on direct examination

imaging.preferred_when: Rarely, when an intraocular mass such as retinoblastoma must be excluded

findings.text: No intraocular mass; retinal changes consistent with ROP

initial.why: The diagnostic test; identifies stage, zone, and plus disease and guides treatment

supporting.why: Shows retinal detachment when the retina cannot be seen directly
supporting.only_if: media opacity or poor dilation prevents adequate fundoscopy

not_indicated.why: Not needed unless an intraocular mass is suspected
not_indicated.only_if: leukocoria or another finding raises concern for retinoblastoma

decision_points: Screen all infants born before 30–32 weeks gestation or with birth weight under 1500 g, and selected larger or more mature infants with an unstable course
First examination at 4–6 weeks postnatal age or 31–33 weeks postmenstrual age, whichever is later
Repeat examinations at intervals set by the findings until retinal vascularization is complete or treatment is given
Type 1 ROP (zone I any stage with plus disease, zone I stage 3 without plus, or zone II stage 2 or 3 with plus) is treated; milder disease is observed
Treatment is usually laser photocoagulation of the avascular retina; intravitreal anti-VEGF is an alternative, especially for zone I disease

criteria.name: International classification of ROP
criteria.summary: ROP is described by the zone of the retina involved (I, II, III), the stage of the vascular abnormality (1 demarcation line, 2 ridge, 3 fibrovascular proliferation, 4 partial retinal detachment, 5 total retinal detachment), and the presence of plus disease (marked posterior vessel dilation and tortuosity).
items: Zone I: posterior retina within 60 degrees of the optic disc
Zone II: from zone I to the nasal ora serrata
Plus disease: dilation and tortuosity of posterior retinal vessels

differential.name: Retinoblastoma
differential.why_considered: Leukocoria or poor visual tracking in an infant; the most important intraocular malignancy of infancy
differential.trigger: Leukocoria, strabismus, or an intraocular mass in an infant

history: May occur in a full-term infant without prematurity or oxygen exposure
Usually no history of prematurity or NICU course
exam: Leukocoria is often the presenting sign
White mass arising from the retina on fundoscopy
May have no plus disease or demarcation line
labs: Genetic testing for RB1 mutation when hereditary disease is suspected
imaging: Ocular ultrasound shows an intraocular mass with calcification
MRI shows a retinal mass and can assess optic nerve or CNS involvement

differential.name: Familial exudative vitreoretinopathy
differential.why_considered: Peripheral retinal avascularity and neovascular changes that mimic ROP

history: Family history of similar retinal disease
May occur in full-term infants without oxygen exposure
exam: Peripheral retinal avascularity with exudation or traction
Findings may be asymmetric and progressive beyond the neonatal period
imaging: Fluorescein angiography shows peripheral avascular retina and leakage
Ocular ultrasound may show retinal detachment or exudate

differential.name: Persistent fetal vasculature
differential.why_considered: Leukocoria, poor vision, or retinal detachment in an infant

history: Often noted at birth or in early infancy
exam: Retrolental fibrovascular membrane or persistent hyaloid stalk
Cataract or anterior segment abnormalities may be present
imaging: Ultrasound shows a retrolental mass or persistent hyaloid artery
MRI can help distinguish from retinoblastoma

differential.name: Congenital cataract
differential.why_considered: Leukocoria or poor visual response in an infant

history: May be present at birth in a full-term infant
May be associated with metabolic or genetic syndromes
exam: Opacification of the lens on slit-lamp or direct ophthalmoscopy
Red reflex is diminished or absent
imaging: Ocular ultrasound is normal posteriorly unless other anomalies coexist

differential.name: Retinal detachment from other causes
differential.why_considered: Retinal detachment is the severe end of ROP and can also occur from other pediatric causes

history: Trauma, prior ocular surgery, or known genetic syndrome
No history of prematurity or oxygen therapy
exam: Retinal detachment without the characteristic demarcation line, ridge, or plus disease of ROP
May have associated ocular trauma signs
imaging: B-scan ultrasound confirms detachment and helps identify underlying cause

severity.mild: Stage 1 or 2 disease in zone II or III without plus disease; often regresses spontaneously with no visual sequelae
severity.moderate: Stage 2 or 3 disease in zone II with or without plus disease, or stage 3 in zone I without plus; requires close monitoring and may need treatment
severity.severe: Type 1 ROP: zone I any stage with plus disease, zone I stage 3 without plus, or zone II stage 2 or 3 with plus disease; treatment with laser or anti-VEGF is indicated to prevent detachment
severity.critical: Stage 4 or 5 ROP with partial or total retinal detachment; risk of permanent blindness and need for surgical intervention

red_flags.finding: Plus disease (marked dilation and tortuosity of posterior retinal vessels)
red_flags.meaning: Severe, treatment-requiring ROP; urgent ophthalmology referral and treatment
Posterior involvement carries a high risk of rapid progression to detachment
Type 1 ROP; laser or anti-VEGF treatment is indicated
Possible retinal detachment or an alternative diagnosis such as retinoblastoma; urgent evaluation

red_flags.finding: Poor visual tracking or nystagmus in an infant with a history of prematurity
red_flags.meaning: May indicate advanced or untreated ROP with visual impairment

complications.name: Retinal detachment
clues: Progression from stage 3 to stage 4 or 5

complications.name: High myopia
clues: Need for glasses at a young age

special_populations.differences: The only population affected; all infants born before 30–32 weeks gestation or under 1500 g birth weight require screening. Even advanced disease is usually asymptomatic, so detection depends on scheduled examinations.

Older children with a history of prematurity may present with strabismus, nystagmus, poor vision, or leukocoria if ROP was not detected or treated in infancy. They require long-term ophthalmologic follow-up for refractive errors, amblyopia, and late complications.

key_questions.question: How early was your baby born, and what was the birth weight?
key_questions.looking_for: Birth before 30–32 weeks gestation and/or weight under 1500 g, which are the main screening criteria

key_questions.question: How many weeks pregnant were you when you delivered?
key_questions.looking_for: Gestational age at birth; lower gestational age means higher risk and earlier screening

key_questions.question: Did your baby need extra oxygen or a breathing machine after birth?
key_questions.looking_for: Supplemental oxygen or mechanical ventilation, a recognized risk factor

key_questions.question: Has your baby had the scheduled eye examinations in the NICU or eye clinic?
key_questions.looking_for: Whether ROP screening has been done and whether follow-up exams were kept

key_questions.question: Has anyone noticed that your baby does not seem to follow faces or light?
key_questions.looking_for: Poor visual tracking, which suggests more advanced disease

key_questions.question: Have you noticed the eyes crossing or moving back and forth on their own?
key_questions.looking_for: Strabismus or nystagmus, which can accompany severe ROP

key_questions.question: Have you ever seen a white glow in the pupil, especially in photos?
key_questions.looking_for: Leukocoria, which suggests retinal detachment or an alternative diagnosis such as retinoblastoma

key_questions.question: Was your baby born as part of a multiple pregnancy (twins, triplets)?
key_questions.looking_for: Multiple gestation, a minor risk factor

key_questions.question: Did your baby have any other problems in the NICU, such as infection, bleeding in the brain, or bowel problems?
key_questions.looking_for: Neonatal sepsis, intraventricular hemorrhage, or necrotizing enterocolitis, which are associated with ROP

key_questions.question: Does anyone in the family have a history of eye problems in infancy or childhood, such as cataracts or retinal disease?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history suggesting an inherited retinal disorder or congenital cataract rather than ROP

key_questions.question: Has your baby been feeding well, gaining weight, and acting normally?
key_questions.looking_for: Reassuring general health; poor feeding or lethargy would suggest another systemic problem

key_questions.question: Any eye redness, discharge, tearing, or pain?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; these suggest infection or another ocular cause rather than ROP

reasoning_points: Infant born prematurely, especially before 30–32 weeks gestation or under 1500 g birth weight
History of supplemental oxygen or mechanical ventilation in the neonatal period
Condition detected on routine ROP screening eye examination rather than from symptoms
Dilated indirect ophthalmoscopy shows a demarcation line, ridge, or fibrovascular proliferation at the junction of vascularized and avascular retina
Plus disease (posterior retinal vessel dilation and tortuosity) indicates severe, treatment-requiring disease
Findings are described by zone, stage, and presence of plus disease using the international classification
Alternative diagnoses such as retinoblastoma, familial exudative vitreoretinopathy, persistent fetal vasculature, and congenital cataract are considered and excluded

easy: Very premature infant (under 30 weeks) with a birth weight under 1500 g
ROP found on the scheduled screening eye examination
Dilated fundoscopy shows a classic demarcation line or ridge
No visual symptoms; the diagnosis is made on screening
medium: Infant with plus disease and stage 3 findings requiring urgent treatment
Asymmetric disease between the two eyes
Larger or more mature premature infant who still meets screening criteria
Infant with other NICU complications such as bronchopulmonary dysplasia or intraventricular hemorrhage
hard: Older infant with a history of prematurity presenting with strabismus, nystagmus, or poor vision after missed screening
Leukocoria in an infant, requiring distinction from retinoblastoma
Full-term infant with retinal findings mimicking ROP, suggesting familial exudative vitreoretinopathy or persistent fetal vasculature
Retinal detachment where the underlying cause is unclear
